introduction: The guide was spoken and written by a man of the East to audiences in the West and to friends in both, in the years around his journeys of 1911 to 1913. It says that East and West are only names; that each has what the other lacks, the one spiritual teaching and the other science and industry; that letters, visits, translations and friendships are the practical means of bringing them together; and that they will one day embrace. A hundred of its quotations are read here with a hundred from elsewhere. Scripture already speaks of light from the east, of many coming from east and west, of walls of partition broken down, and the Qur’an says that East and West belong to God and that peoples were made different in order to know one another. Paul’s letters and journeys, which first carried a faith from Asia into Europe, are the nearest earlier parallel, and are used for the passages on correspondence and travel. Confucius, Marcus Aurelius, Whitman, Twain and Vivekananda speak for the same widening. The age’s own voices are placed where they are needed: Kipling’s famous line and his ‘burden’, Macaulay’s contempt for Eastern learning, Thucydides on the strong and the weak, Twain on the export of civilization, Gandhi’s judgement of the West, and Lao Tzu’s doubt that peoples need to meet at all.
questions: The guide says East and West are imaginary words. What real differences does it nevertheless describe, and how does it want them used?
Kipling's line 'never the twain shall meet' and Macaulay's judgement of Eastern literature were written in the same age as these talks. What did the guide's hearers have to unlearn?
The guide proposes an exchange: spiritual teaching from the East, science from the West. Is that division fair to either, then or now?
Thucydides and Twain point to power. Can peoples meet as friends while one rules the other?
Much of the guide is about letters, visits and translations. Which ordinary means of connection between distant peoples do you take for granted, and which do you neglect?
The Qur'an says peoples were made different so that they might know one another. What have you learned about your own culture from knowing someone of another?

outside.why: Kipling's ballad opens with the line everyone remembers: East is East, and West is West, and never the twain shall meet. Why has that line been remembered and the lines that follow it forgotten?
Whitman saw in the works of his age God's purpose from the first: the earth to be spanned, the races neighbours, the distant brought near.
Paul says of his own divided world that the middle wall of partition has been broken down, and both made one.
The Qur'an says that unto God belong the East and the West, and whithersoever ye turn, there is God's countenance.
The Qur'an's lamp is kindled from a blessed tree, an olive neither of the East nor of the West.
Jesus says that many shall come from the east and west and sit down together in the kingdom of heaven.
Paul asks one church to supply another's want from its abundance, and expects the same in return.
Paul, turned back from Asia, sees a man of Macedonia in a vision saying: come over and help us.
Montaigne found that every one gives the title of barbarism to everything that is not in use in his own country.
At Pentecost Parthians, Medes, Elamites and men of Rome and Arabia each hear in their own tongue.
Zechariah hears how such things are done: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.
The psalm exclaims how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
Hebrews asks its readers not to be forgetful to entertain strangers, since some have entertained angels unawares.
One who sat at meat with Jesus said: blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God.
Confucius asks whether it is not delightful to have friends coming from distant quarters.
A disciple of Confucius says that for the reverent and courteous all within the four seas will be brothers.
Ruth, a foreigner, says to Naomi: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.
The Qur'an counts the difference of languages and colours among the signs of God.
Mark Twain observed that travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry and narrow-mindedness.
Kipling urged the West to take up the White Man's burden and serve its captives' need. What did the East have reason to feel about Westerners who came in that spirit?
Paul writes to a distant church that though absent in the flesh he is with them in the spirit.
Paul speaks of being taken from his friends in presence, not in heart.
Donne says that two souls which are one endure not a breach by distance, but an expansion.
Paul's image for those who are of one breath is the body, which is one and has many members.
Paul tells a church of mixed origins that they are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens.
Paul asks that his letter be read in one church and exchanged with the next.
Proverbs says that good news from a far country is as cold waters to a thirsty soul.
Paul calls his friends an epistle written in his heart, known and read of all men.
The elder writes that he has many things to say, and would rather speak face to face.
Paul thanks his God upon every remembrance of his friends in a far city.
Paul, long hindered, plans to see the Romans on his journey westward into Spain.
Paul longs to see the Romans so that he and they may be comforted together by their mutual faith.
Goethe said that a man who has no acquaintance with foreign languages knows nothing of his own.
Isaiah foresees a dawn in which nations beat their swords into plowshares.
The Qur'an says that humankind was made nations and tribes in order that they may know one another.
UNESCO's constitution names ignorance of each other's ways and lives as a common cause of suspicion and mistrust between peoples.
Garrison's motto was: our country is the world, our countrymen are mankind.
Tocqueville observed how much is done in America by associations of every kind.
Jesus likens the kingdom to a mustard seed, least of seeds, which becomes the greatest among herbs.
Thucydides records the doctrine that the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must. Can there be cooperation between East and West while one holds power over the other?
The queen of Sheba, hearing of Solomon's fame, came from afar to prove him with hard questions.
Proverbs says that iron sharpeneth iron, so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
Mill held that he who knows only his own side of the case knows little of that.
Macaulay claimed that a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia. What must change in such a mind before any exchange of gifts is possible?
Matthew's Gospel begins with wise men who came from the east, following a star.
Carlyle wrote of the Arabs and their Prophet as a spark fallen on what seemed black unnoticeable sand.
Arnold called faith in machinery the besetting danger of his own country.
Ezekiel sees the glory of God come from the way of the east, and the earth shine with it.
The Qur'an says that it is not righteousness to turn your faces to the East and the West, but to believe and to do good.
Malachi hears that from the rising of the sun to its going down the name shall be great among the nations.
Jeremiah says that the word was in his heart as a burning fire shut up in his bones.
Jesus says that the wind bloweth where it listeth, and none can tell whence it comes or whither it goes.
The psalm says that from the rising of the sun unto its going down the Lord's name is to be praised.
Malachi promises that the Sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in his wings.
This is the saying: as the lightning cometh out of the east, and shineth even unto the west.
Paul speaks of the savour of knowledge made manifest in every place.
In Acts the witnesses are sent from Jerusalem to the uttermost part of the earth.
Zacharias sings of the dayspring from on high that gives light to them that sit in darkness.
Isaiah hears: I will bring thy seed from the east, and gather thee from the west.
Habakkuk foresees the earth filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.
Jesus says that he has other sheep not of this fold, and that there shall be one fold and one shepherd.
Jesus observed, with a solemn 'verily I say unto you', that no prophet is accepted in his own country.
In the parable the same seed bears differently according to the ground it falls on.

Jesus tells his hearers that the kingdom shall be given to a nation bringing forth its fruits. What does it mean for a message to be more effective away from where it arose, and how should either place feel about that?
Twain wrote bitterly of the Blessings-of-Civilization Trust to which the rulers of Christendom belong. What did the West owe the East in an age when it held it captive?
Aristotle held that whoever bids the law rule bids God and Reason alone rule.
Vivekananda held that each tradition must assimilate the spirit of the others and yet grow according to its own law.
Shelley's traveller from an antique land finds a king's boast on a pedestal, and the lone and level sands.

Gandhi judged modern civilization to be such that one has only to be patient and it will be self-destroyed. Is the guide's judgement of European materialism the same as his, or does it leave more hope?
Wordsworth says of his own country that the world is too much with us, and that getting and spending we lay waste our powers.
The Qur'an has believers say that they make no distinction between any of God's messengers.
Jesus says that many prophets and righteous men desired to see what his hearers see, and did not.
Rumi says that the lamps are different but the Light is the same: it comes from Beyond.
Malachi asks: have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?
Acts says that God has made of one blood all nations of men to dwell on all the face of the earth.
John's letter says that whoever does not love a brother he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen.
The psalm makes harmony a thing to be worked for: depart from evil, do good, seek peace and pursue it.
Ashoka's edict says that whoever praises his own religion and condemns others only harms his own.
Isaiah hears that the house shall be called an house of prayer for all people.
Jesus tells his followers that they are the light of the world.
The psalm has its own embrace: mercy and truth are met together, righteousness and peace have kissed each other.
Tennyson foresaw the battle-flags furled in the Parliament of man, the Federation of the world.
Isaiah pictures the wolf dwelling with the lamb and the leopard lying down with the kid.
Victor Hugo told the nations of Europe that a day would come when they would be one without losing their distinctive qualities.
Lao Tzu's ideal is neighbouring states within sight of one another whose people never meet. Is it certain that peoples are better for being brought together?
The psalm takes east and west as the measure of the greatest distance there is. What had to change in the world for that distance to become a matter of days, and what has not changed with it?
The Qur'an tells believers to hold fast together and remember that they were enemies and were made brothers.
Marcus Aurelius says that as Antoninus his city is Rome, but as a man it is the world.
John sees a great multitude of all nations, kindreds, peoples and tongues standing together.
Paul says that by one Spirit all are baptized into one body, whatever their origin.
Daniel says that they that turn many to righteousness shall shine as the stars for ever and ever.
Isaiah promises that the Lord of hosts shall make unto all people a feast.
The Qur'an says that God will perfect his light, however much it is opposed.
The Song of Solomon hears the time of the singing of birds come, and the voice of the turtle in the land.
Isaiah foresees the wilderness glad, and the desert rejoicing and blossoming as the rose.
Isaiah has the mountains break forth into singing and the trees of the field clap their hands.
Paul says that if one member suffer, all the members suffer with it.
Okakura wrote for Western readers of a way of tea that adores the beautiful among the facts of everyday life. What can a small custom carry between civilizations that arguments cannot?
Jesus says that whoever will be great shall be a minister, and gives his own life as the pattern.
In Luke Jesus says that the Spirit of the Lord is upon him, to preach, to heal and to set at liberty.

psalm-as-far-as-the-east-is-from-the-wes.text: As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us

psalm-from-the-rising-of-the-sun.text: From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same the Lord's name is to be praised

isaiah-bring-thy-seed-from-the-east.text: Fear not: for I am with thee: I will bring thy seed from the east, and gather thee from the west; I will say to the north, Give up; and to the south, Keep not back: bring my sons from far, and my daughters from the ends of the earth

acts-parthians-and-medes.text: And they were all amazed and marvelled, saying one to another, Behold, are not all these which speak Galilaeans? And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born? Parthians, and Medes, and Elamites, and the dwellers in Mesopotamia, and in Judaea, and Cappadocia, in Pontus, and Asia, Phrygia, and Pamphylia, in Egypt, and in the parts of Libya about Cyrene, and strangers of Rome, Jews and proselytes, Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God

kings-queen-of-sheba.text: And when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the Lord, she came to prove him with hard questions

analects-all-within-the-four-seas.text: Let the superior man never fail reverentially to order his own conduct, and let him be respectful to others and observant of propriety:-then all within the four seas will be his brothers
analects-all-within-the-four-seas.author: Confucius

marcus-as-a-man-it-is-the-world.text: But my nature is rational and social; and my city and country, so far as I am Antoninus, is Rome, but so far as I am a man, it is the world
marcus-as-a-man-it-is-the-world.author: Marcus Aurelius
